entries.title: U.S. Ready to Slap Tariffs on China, EU and Others: AP Sources
entries.summary: The Trump administration is pushing the tariffs over what it says are subsidized production in 16 economies.
entries.content:
By Chris Rugaber, Aamer Madhani and Josh Boak

The Trump administration is expected to soon announce plans to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and 14 other economies, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The U.S. Trade Representative's Office is expected to release the results of a monthslong tariff investigation into the industrial subsidies by the 16 economies in the coming days, according to the people who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

They stressed the timing for the rollout of the tariffs could still change. The White House and USTR did not respond to requests for comment.

Plans for the new tariffs are part of an effort to replace broader duties the administration set last year that were subsequently struck down by the Supreme Court. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.

The tariffs are in response to what the White House has said is excessive manufacturing output in those countries, boosted by subsidies, that has led to a flood of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies.

The anticipated action constitutes a second step in the administration’s efforts to replace the duties announced in April 2025 that the Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional in February. The White House slapped 60 trading partners with levies of 10% to 12.5% in July, charging that they have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.

The anticipated trade action demonstrates that the Trump administration is still willing to impose import taxes despite a sweeping loss for the Republican Party in this month’s midterm elections, fueled largely by affordability concerns as inflation remains elevated. At the same time, the new duties could test how the Democrats will respond to tariffs imposed unilaterally by Trump.

Even with majorities in both the House and Senate, Trump could veto any legislation that overturns or waters down the tariffs.

The excess industrial capacity probes were initiated under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the president to levy tariffs against nations that discriminate against U.S. companies or commerce.

The levels of the anticipated tariffs were not immediately clear, but would come on top of tariffs of 10% to 12.5% announced earlier this year.

Many countries, including China, had protested those tariffs, which took effect just as the clock ran out on temporary levies Trump had turned to after the Supreme Court in February struck down sweeping “reciprocal” tariffs he levied on nearly every U.S. trade partner.

The expected move comes as Trump just last week visited the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen for his third face-to-face engagement with Chinese President Xi Jinping this year. Xi’s expected to travel to Doral, Florida, next month for the Group of 20 Summit, which Trump is hosting.

While Trump has moved to build a closer relationship with Xi, the yawning trade deficit remains a significant irritant in the U.S.-China relationship.

Massive capacity in a slew of Chinese industries, from autos to solar panels, cement and steel manufacturing, has drawn increased attention from Beijing’s trading partners in recent years.

Although China’s own leaders have prioritized rebalancing the economy, slowing domestic demand has prompted companies to expand into overseas markets. Surging exports pushed China’s trade surplus to a record of nearly $1.2 trillion last year.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Signature Move
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Nov. 25, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Claims of “fraudulent activity,” cancer scam allegations and a clutch rookie. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 6/10. A tranquil travel day with partial sun filtered by increasing clouds. No rain or strong wind worries until the night. Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

A new shot has been fired in the D.C. wage wars.

Opponents of a proposed initiative that would increase the minimum wage in D.C. to $25 are challenging tens of thousands of voter signatures submitted by the initiative’s proponents, including thousands they say were obtained fraudulently, The Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports.

The challenge is being brought by attorneys who work closely with the Restaurant Association of Metropolitan Washington, which is leading the fight against Initiative 87. They are challenging more than 30,000 of the 43,000 signatures submitted; it would need valid signatures from 22,471 D.C. voters to remain on the ballot.

“Every petition drive produces some bad signatures. That’s expected. What we found goes far beyond that. The scale of what we uncovered points to systemic fraudulent activity,” said Andrew Kline, the attorney leading the challenge.

The challenge alleges that two petition circulators who collected more than 8,200 signatures forged some of their submissions. “I’m rather angry,” D.C. resident Mark Lyon told The Sun after finding what he says was a traced version of his signature on a petition he did not sign.

But there are other problems with many signatures, said Kline — so many that Initiative 87 wouldn’t meet the threshold to make the ballot, he contends.

“We’re confident we collected enough valid signatures to qualify for April,” said Mariah Ross of One Fair Wage, the New York-based group behind Initiative 87. “If opponents believe $25 an hour is too much for the people who cook our meals and serve our tables, they should make that case in public and let D.C. voters decide in April.”

The D.C. Board of Elections will have 20 days to review the challenge and decide whether Initiative 87 can go to voters. If it decides it can’t, it won’t be the first time a D.C. ballot initiative has been done in by fraud allegations — it also happened in 2004 with an initiative that sought to legalize slot machines in the District.





DEEP DIVE

The U.S. Education Department has designated Virginia’s entire public school system as “high-risk,” a status that could lower the state’s ability to compete for federal grant funds, The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports. The department cited the failure of Albemarle County School District in central Virginia to properly screen more than 500 staff members over three years, including not verifying “whether they had a history of child abuse or neglect.”

Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s office said it has contacted its school divisions to ensure they comply with mandatory reporting processes and will pursue statewide corrective action.

“Regrettably, President Trump’s Department of Education is threatening federal education dollars for every student in every public school across Virginia, which does nothing to keep kids safe,” the governor’s office said in a statement.

Alexandria City Public Schools told parents on Monday that after conducting its own internal review, it had placed 72 of its employees on leave due to incomplete background checks, WJLA reports. The discrepancies date as far back as 2023. The school system said 27 employees have since been cleared to return to work. Employees yet to be cleared may be placed in non-student-facing roles.





FROM THE DISTRICT

The Trump administration is requesting $100 million from Congress to expedite redevelopment of the Southwest Federal Center area, The Sun’s Jenny Gathright reports. Local officials have long wanted to redevelop that swath of underutilized federal buildings into a vibrant new neighborhood — but D.C. Del.-elect Robert White said he wants to make sure D.C. officials will have a say in how the money is spent.

Plans to redevelop a Tenleytown bank building into an “urban mall” might be on the rocks, as historic preservationists have nominated the site for inclusion on the National Register of Historic Places, the Washington Business Journal reports.

Howard University Hospital ranked among the worst in the nation for patient safety, according to an analysis by a D.C.-based nonprofit watchdog, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports. Out of nearly 2,400 hospitals reviewed, Howard’s hospital was one of just three to get an “F” grade.





FROM VIRGINIA

The Army intends to resume helicopter training flights near National Airport, less than two years after the deadly crash between a Black Hawk helicopter and an American Airlines regional jet that killed 67 people, The Sun’s Gavin J. Quinton reports.





FROM MARYLAND

A Howard County judge ordered that a woman accused of spending $200,000 in donations she received for faked cancer treatment on trips, clothes and entertainment be released on bail, The Baltimore Banner reports. Prosecutors argue that Lexi Thomas duped friends, neighbors and even her own husband with a yearslong cancer scam using manipulated images, and by claiming she had to go unaccompanied to treatments in an experimental clinical trial.

A man from Prince George’s County with Alzheimer’s disease who went missing last week was found hours later, playing a piano left out on a front lawn near his childhood home in Philadelphia, NBC4 reports.





PLAN YOUR WEEKEND


US Botanic Garden holiday show (7360x4912, AR: 1.50)
For the festive: “Season’s Greenings” at the U.S. Botanic Garden, tomorrow through Jan. 3.

For the merry: “Drunk Christmas Carol” at the Sage Theatre, through Jan. 3.

For Alicia Keys fans: “Hell’s Kitchen” at the National Theatre, through Dec. 6.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

So, how did the Commanders pull off a 22-20 upset of the Bengals? The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson studied the tape and highlights a few quiet catalysts, including an improved run game and a savvy young linebacker.

When the Commanders were at their most desperate Monday night, it was rookie receiver Antonio Williams who came up big. The third-round pick from Clemson finished with nine catches for 122 yards. He capped the best performance of his young career with a stunning 42-yard reception that set Washington up for the game-winning field goal. The Sun’s Noah Ferguson writes that teammates and coaches were not surprised to see the 22-year-old meet the moment.

“He was just clutch tonight,” coach Dan Quinn said. “Made some big plays in some big moments. He’s demonstrated that in a lot of instances, so it was good to see him deliver tonight.”

What to Watch Today

NHL: Capitals vs. Flyers, 7 p.m. (Monumental)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

Programming note: No newsletter the next two days — we will be back Monday. Happy Thanksgiving!

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson.

entries.title: U.S. Army Detonates Degrading Lead Explosives in Iowa
entries.summary: People living in the path of the projected lead dust plume were given evacuation orders.
entries.content:
The U.S. Army detonated nearly five tons of lead explosives in Middletown, Iowa, on Wednesday morning, but it has not yet said whether an expected plume of lead dust spread into the atmosphere in the aftermath.

The Army said it would provide an update no later than two hours after the explosion.

Many people living in the path of the projected lead dust plume — stretching across southeastern Iowa and northeastern Missouri — have evacuated and are awaiting instructions from the Army about returning to their homes.

The Army and the Environmental Protection Agency, along with outside researchers, will be taking air and soil samples to measure where lead dust is still in the air and where it has fallen to the ground. The government has pledged to offer tests to anyone who wants them and to remediate areas where lead concentrations are found to be above federally acceptable levels.

Gov. Kim Reynolds issued a disaster emergency proclamation for Des Moines, Lee and Van Buren counties Tuesday night, sending 100 members of the National Guard to support the Army’s planned detonation.

Across southeast Iowa and into Missouri, small towns prepared for the detonation by closing schools and businesses and canceling activities. Officials also handed out brochures detailing emergency resources. Some buildings, like the Salvation Army near Burlington, were opened as shelters.

It was a Thanksgiving disruption for Middletown resident Stacey Waterman, who told The Washington Sun she planned to evacuate to her parents’ house in Illinois on Wednesday morning before returning to Middletown to assess any damage to her home.

“I think we just have to trust our leadership, right? We have to trust that they’ve done their due diligence in making sure that the people are as safe as they can,” Waterman told The Sun Tuesday evening. “I think they evaluated as many options as they possibly could and chose what they felt was the best one. And we all just have to pray that it’s the right thing and that nobody ends up hurt out of this in the end.”

The Army followed through with its plan to deliberately detonate 68 barrels of degrading lead azide on Wednesday after repeatedly delaying its plans. Originally scheduled for last Friday, the Trump administration faced public outrage over the government’s limited communications about the plan and its possible risks.

The Trump administration said that it needed to deliberately blow up the country’s stockpile of lead explosives because they were rapidly degrading, forming crystals that were increasingly likely to self-detonate as temperatures fell in Middletown. “There is consensus across the experts across the country that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation,” Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said at a press conference Tuesday.

The Washington Sun reported that Reynolds and local Iowa communities were only given five days’ notice of the originally scheduled detonation. Officials in Illinois, parts of which were a possible risk area for a toxic plume, said they were not informed at all.

Amid public panic, the Trump administration mobilized a whole-of-government response, enlisting the Environmental Protection Agency, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, the Centers for Disease Control, the National Weather Service, the Department of Energy and even two NASA aircraft.

The government also dramatically increased its efforts to reduce the possibility of a lead dust plume. On Monday night, the Army built a dam around the explosives designed to flood the area with water and foam just ahead of the explosion in an effort to weigh down and absorb any escaping lead dust.

“This is an unprecedented amount of both protection works and mitigation measures,” Col. Aaron C. Teller, the commander of the 71st Ordnance Group and in charge of planning the controlled detonation, said at a Tuesday press conference. “Our goal is to get to zero, zero release.”

Almost all of the Army’s entire stockpile of lead azide sat in storage, unused, at the Iowa plant for the last 20 years.

With the detonation now past, locals and officials in Washington, D.C., are asking how the Army reached the point of needing to blow up the lead azide in the first place.

Army officials discovered that the explosives had already deteriorated so much that they could not be moved or treated in March, but the Army still has not answered questions about whether the explosives were degrading before March.

“There must be a thorough investigation with real accountability to ensure this never happens again in Iowa or anywhere else in the country,” said Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson in a statement.

Other members of Congress on both sides of the aisle have also called for investigations, and the Trump administration said it will begin looking into the government contractor responsible for managing the explosive.
entries.author: Anna Kramer, Will Hofmann
